report: The patient’s stridor and increased work of breathing localize obstruction to the supraglottis. The history of falling with an e-cigarette in the mouth and possible loss of consciousness provides a clear traumatic/thermal mechanism. CT showing glottic/supraglottic swelling without fractures and laryngoscopy showing diffuse edema with mucosal sloughing—interpreted by the radiologist as thermal injury—strongly support supraglottic traumatic edema. Infectious supraglottitis is unlikely given no infectious features and the thermal injury pattern; foreign-body obstruction is excluded by lack of a discrete object on CT/laryngoscopy. Thus the evidence converges on supraglottic traumatic edema.
answer: Chemical burns of the pharynx and esophagus due to e-cigarette injury
